body:
FOUND by two P5 lenses on T177 (2026-08-17), both CONFIRMED by tracing and by live probes. Two faults
that share one root: the store now advertises a PER-MOUNT resource identity that the rest of the door
does not yet honour. Both need Myk, for different reasons.

PART A — THE CHALLENGE AND THE DOCUMENT DISAGREE, AND STRICT CLIENTS TAKE THE CHALLENGE ROUTE.
T177 added per-mount documents at RFC 9728's path-inserted URI, each naming that mount's endpoint as
`resource`. But `challengeFor` still points every 401 at the BARE store-wide document, whose
`resource` is the origin. So one door answers two different identifiers for the same resource:

  self-constructed route (what Claude does):  /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/garden/mcp
                                              resource = https://host/garden/mcp        MATCHES
  challenge route (RFC 9728 §5.1):            /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
                                              resource = https://host                   MISMATCH

RFC 9728 §3.3 tells a client to REJECT a document whose `resource` does not match the URL it is
accessing. This is NOT a regression — before T177 the single document failed that check for every
mount — and the measured client self-constructs, which is why T177 fixed the observed failure. But a
strict client that follows the header rather than building the path gets the mismatching document, and
that is the one user-visible correctness gap the connector arc has left.

WHY IT COULD NOT SHIP WITH T177, and this is the part that needs a decision rather than a rename:
T133 froze the challenge in three places in `test/server/oauth-discovery.test.ts` — (a), (h) and (l) —
plus an exact literal in `test/cli/serve-public-url.test.ts`. Rail (h) is not a byte pin: it asserts
the challenge is IDENTICAL across a public mount, a private mount and an absent one. A per-mount
challenge makes those three differ, so a `rail-renames.json` substitution cannot rescue it — the
exemption is for a vocabulary rename, and this would rewrite what the rail MEASURES. It also
contradicts a promise T133 states in words: the challenge is a constant of the server, blind to the
mount. Changing it is a DECIDE.

THE DECISION (Myk): may the challenge name the refused mount's document?
  Recommendation: YES, and the oracle objection does not survive scrutiny. The challenge would echo a
  mount name THE CALLER ALREADY SUPPLIED, and T177's document answers 200 for a ghost mount exactly as
  it does for a live one (measured: byte-identical status, headers and body modulo the supplied name).
  So a per-mount challenge discloses nothing a prober did not already hold. What it buys is
  conformance for clients that follow the header — the route the RFC actually prescribes.
  If NO: say so in §37, and the store accepts that strict clients cannot use the challenge route.

PART B — `resource` IS ADVERTISED AND ENFORCED NOWHERE (RFC 8707).
The per-mount document tells a client its token is for `https://host/garden/mcp`. Nothing accepts or
checks that: `makeConsentDoor.handleGet` reads only `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `state`,
`code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method`; the token door mints nothing mount-scoped; `identify`
resolves a connector token to an actor with no mount in view, and the mount is taken from the path
afterwards. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: a token consented against `resource=<origin>/garden/mcp` works on
`/meadow/mcp`.

This is NOT privilege escalation — in-gateway grants still gate what that actor may do at either
mount — but it is a document making a per-resource claim the door does not enforce, which is H7's
shape on the discovery surface. Two honest ways out, and the ticket wants one chosen:
  (a) ENFORCE IT: accept `resource` at the authorize door per RFC 8707, carry it on the code and the
      token, and refuse a token presented at a mount it was not consented for. This makes the
      advertised identity real and gives an operator per-mount connector scoping, which is a genuine
      capability rather than a repair.
  (b) SAY SO: state in §37 that `resource` identifies the door for discovery only and is not a token
      audience, and that a connector's reach is bounded by its grants rather than by the mount it was
      consented at. Cheapest, and honest.
  Recommendation: (b) now, (a) as its own ticket if per-mount connector scoping is ever wanted. Do not
  leave it unsaid — an integrator reading the document will assume an audience.

RAILS, whichever way each part goes:
- Part A YES: the challenge names the refused mount's document; following it unauthenticated answers
  200; the document's `resource` equals the URL the client dialed; and the GHOST rail still holds, so
  the challenge cannot become an enumeration oracle. Plus the T133 authorization pairs, two PRs.
- Part A NO: a rail asserting the challenge stays constant across mounts, and a §37 sentence saying
  the challenge route is not conformant for a mount-scoped resource.
- Part B (a): a token consented at one mount is REFUSED at another, two-sided with a bystander mount
  that still works.
- Part B (b): a §37 sentence, and nothing to rail — but the sentence must exist before the spec
  section for T177 lands, or the section overclaims by omission.
title: The per-mount resource identity is advertised but not honoured — the challenge points elsewhere, and nothing enforces it as an audience
